haiku-low.q1: The replica's reports.row_count decides: 10,000 or fewer streams CSV in the same response; more queues a background job, emails a download link, and the page shows status.
haiku-low.q2: The click gets back the existing queued or running export, with HTTP 202, even if its filters differ. No new export starts.
haiku-low.q3: The emailed link works 24 hours. The exports bucket rule deletes the object 7 days after creation. Export rows are kept, and there is no cleanup job.
haiku-low.q4: Three attempts, retried after 60 s and 300 s. After the third failure the page shows Export failed with Try again, and the user gets an export_failed email.
haiku-low.q5: Report rows are read from the read replica. Export records are written to the primary. Which database the permission checks and row_count read use is NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q6: In the report_exports table on the primary database. The page calls the latest endpoint on load or return, and every 5 seconds while queued or running.
haiku-low.q7: It reads 500-row pages by keyset paging, writes CSV into a 16 MB buffer, and uploads each full buffer as a multipart part, keeping only etags. Memory stays well under 512 MB.
haiku-low.q8: On a handled failure the upload is aborted, best effort. If the worker dies, unfinished parts expire after 24 hours. The next attempt starts a new upload from row one.
haiku-low.q9: The filters and cols are saved on the report_exports row when the click inserts it. The job payload carries only export_id, and the handler reads the row from the primary.
haiku-low.q10: A partial unique index on (user_id, report_id) where status is queued or running. A click that loses the insert race reads and returns the winning row.
haiku-low.q11: The file must be completed and the row set to done with object_key. A rerun on done with email_sent_at set returns. Done without it resends the email only, without rebuilding.
haiku-low.q12: The browser saves only after the full body arrives. A cut-off body throws, nothing is saved, and the user can click again. Server-side handling: NOT STATED.

sonnet.q1: Server reads reports.row_count (unfiltered total) from the replica. 10,000 rows or fewer: small path, CSV streamed in the same response (text/csv attachment, no job, no stored file). Larger: large path, HTTP 202 with JSON (export_id, status, filters, cols); a background job builds the file, stores it in the exports bucket, and emails a 24-hour download link.
sonnet.q2: The click returns the existing queued/running export (even if its filters differ from the page's); no new export or job is created. A new one starts only after the old is done or failed, or is stale (then marked failed with 'could not queue' and replaced). Open question 6 asks whether to return 409 instead.
sonnet.q3: The link lasts 86,400 seconds (24 hours). The bucket's rules delete each object 7 days after creation (and discard uploads not completed within 24 hours). Export rows are kept; no cleanup job.
sonnet.q4: Up to 3 attempts total (retries after 60 s, then 300 s). After the third failure the final-failure handler runs once: it marks the row failed (unless already done) with the error cut to 500 chars, aborts any saved upload best-effort, and sends an 'export_failed' email. The page shows 'Export failed' with a Try again button. (If the export was already done, it stays done and no failure email is sent.)
sonnet.q5: The read replica (read-only). Report rows are read only from the replica; export records are on the primary.
sonnet.q6: In the report_exports table (export record) on the primary database. The page calls GET /api/reports/{report_id}/exports/latest on load or when the user returns (read from the primary, newest export for the user and report), and polls it every 5 seconds while queued or running, stopping at done or failed. On failure of a call it keeps the last known state and shows a retry message.
sonnet.q7: It streams: reads pages of 500 rows from the replica by keyset paging, writes CSV lines into a 16 MB buffer, uploads each full buffer as a multipart part (keeping only the etag), then uploads the remainder as the last part. Memory is one page, one 16 MB buffer and a list of etags, within 512 MB. The whole build must fit in one 30-minute attempt (open question 3 notes risk for 2 million rows; the document does not say whether it fits).
sonnet.q8: Each attempt starts from scratch with a new upload at an attempt-specific key; nothing resumes (resuming is only an unadopted option). If the handler raises, it aborts the upload best-effort. If the worker dies or times out, no code runs and the parts stay until the bucket's 24-hour rule discards them. Nothing is visible until the upload is completed. The next attempt starts again from the first row with a new multipart upload.
sonnet.q9: They are stored in the export row's filters and cols columns (copied from the page URL) in report_exports on the primary. The job payload contains only {"export_id": ...}; the handler reads the row, with user, report, filters and columns, from the primary.
sonnet.q10: A partial unique index on (user_id, report_id) where status is queued or running in report_exports. If an insert hits it, the losing click reads and returns the winning row and enqueues nothing.
sonnet.q11: The file must be fully built and the multipart upload completed, with the row updated to done (object_key set, completed_at set), before the email step; the email uses a 24-hour signed URL. On a rerun: if the row is failed, return; if done and email_sent_at is set, return (duplicate delivery); if done but email_sent_at is empty, skip rebuilding and go straight to emailing. Known gap: if the email is delivered but the process dies before email_sent_at is saved, the user may get the link twice.
sonnet.q12: The response is cut off, so the browser's fetch throws, nothing is saved and the user can click again. No job or stored file exists. If the replica is unavailable the request returns 503 and nothing is written. The document does not describe any other mid-stream handling or server-side cleanup.
